title: Protective devices
summary: Defines overcurrent, overload, fault and earth leakage current, then compares fuses, circuit breakers (Types B, C and D), RCDs and RCBOs.

sections.heading: Overcurrent and earth leakage current
paragraphs: The protective devices in a consumer unit must handle both overcurrent conditions and earth leakage current conditions.
BS 7671 Part 2 defines overcurrent as a current exceeding the rated value; for conductors the rated value is the current-carrying capacity. It is subdivided into overload current and fault current.

Overload current is an overcurrent in a circuit which is electrically sound, so the fault is caused by devices or equipment connected to the installation. Fault current is a current resulting from a fault, for example cable or equipment insulation failure, a motor short circuit, or a short circuit in electronic equipment circuits.

Earth leakage current is called protective conductor current in BS 7671 Part 2: electric current appearing in a protective conductor, such as leakage current or current resulting from an insulation fault. It can range from a few milliamps to hundreds of amps, and protective devices must deal with all conditions.
bullets: Overcurrent: a current exceeding the rated value (for conductors, the current-carrying capacity)
Overcurrent is subdivided into overload current and fault current
Overload current: overcurrent in an electrically sound circuit
Fault current: a current resulting from a fault
Earth leakage current: referred to as protective conductor current
Earth leakage currents range from a few milliamps to hundreds of amps

sections.heading: Fuse terms
paragraphs: A fuse is a device which, by the melting of one or more specially designed and proportioned components, opens the circuit by breaking the current when it exceeds a given value for a sufficient time. The fuse comprises all the parts that form the complete device.

The fuse carrier is the movable part designed to carry a fuse link. The fuse element is the part designed to melt when the fuse operates. The fuse link includes the fuse element(s) and must be replaced by a new or renewable fuse link after the fuse has operated and before it is put back into service.
bullets: Fuse: opens the circuit by melting of its components when current exceeds a given value for a sufficient time
Fuse carrier: movable part designed to carry a fuse link
Fuse element: part designed to melt when the fuse operates
Fuse link: includes the element(s); replaced after operation

sections.heading: BS 88 cartridge fuses
paragraphs: BS 88-3:2010 cartridge fuses replace BS 1361. Advantages: small physical size, no mechanical moving parts, accurate current rating, element enclosed so scattering is prevented, not liable to deterioration with age, and a fusing factor of 1.6-1.9. Disadvantages: more expensive than rewireable, can be bypassed using silver foil, cannot break large fault currents, difficult to see if blown, and can be replaced with an incorrect cartridge.

BS 88-2:2010 fuses replace BS 88-2.2 and BS 88-6. Advantages: no moving parts, very accurate declared rating, very quick operation, and reliable breaking of large currents. With gM fuses you can distinguish between a persistent fault and a transient fault such as the large starting current of motors. Disadvantage: expensive.
Both types are most commonly used as the distributor's fuse. Some types were withdrawn in 2010, but they will be found in older installations for many years.
bullets: BS 88-3:2010 (replaces BS 1361): fusing factor 1.6-1.9
BS 88-3 disadvantages: can be bypassed with silver foil; difficult to see if blown
BS 88-2:2010: quick operation, can break large currents, expensive
gM fuses can tell a persistent fault from a transient fault such as motor starting current
Most commonly used as the distributor's fuse

sections.heading: BS 3036 semi-enclosed fuse
paragraphs: BS 3036 semi-enclosed fuses are rewireable fuses. The colour denotes the rating.

Advantages: simple to check if blown, low cost to replace the element, and no moving parts. Disadvantages: danger of being repaired with the wrong size wire, deterioration with age, circuit cannot be quickly restored, cannot break large fault currents, danger if replaced on a faulty circuit (melting wire), and the element can scatter. They cannot be guaranteed to operate quickly enough for lower value fault currents, so cables protected by them must have a larger current-carrying capacity.
bullets: Rewireable; colour denotes the rating
Advantages: easy to check, cheap element, no moving parts
Disadvantages: wrong wire danger, ageing, slow to restore, element can scatter
Cannot be guaranteed to operate quickly enough for lower value fault currents, so protected cables need larger current-carrying capacity

sections.heading: BS 1362 plug fuses
paragraphs: BS 1362 cartridge fuses break a faulty circuit in the same way as other fuses and are made especially for the standard UK BS 1363 13 A plug top. When the BS 1363 plug was introduced there were five fuses in the range: 2A (blue), 5A (grey), 7A (black), 10A (yellow) and 13A (brown).

The current version, BS 1362:1973, allows any rating up to 13A, with 3A (red) and 13A (brown) as the preferred (but not mandated) values in a plug. The plug fuse protects the flexible cord, not the appliance itself.
bullets: Original range: 2A blue, 5A grey, 7A black, 10A yellow, 13A brown
BS 1362:1973: any rating up to 13A
Preferred: 3A (red) and 13A (brown)
Purpose: protect the flexible cord, not the appliance

sections.heading: Circuit breakers
paragraphs: Circuit breakers to BS EN 60898 use two effects of current. The thermal mechanism operates relatively slowly and suits overload currents. The magnetic mechanism operates very quickly and suits fault currents. A CB (formerly MCB) is commonly used to protect final circuits; an MCCB is used in larger distribution circuits and has a much higher breaking capacity.

Types are based on the ability to handle surge currents without tripping, such as inrush currents from fluorescent lighting, induction motors and battery charging equipment. Type B trips at 3-5 times the rated current (In), so a 10 A device trips at 30 A-50 A; it is generally used in domestic installations or light commercial applications. Type C trips at 5-10 times In (10 A trips at 50 A-100 A) in commercial and industrial applications. Type D trips at 10-20 times In (10 A trips at 100 A-200 A) in industrial applications with high inrush currents, such as large battery charging systems, winding motors, transformers, X-ray machines and some discharge lighting.

BS 7671 Table 41.1 gives maximum disconnection times for final circuits not exceeding 32 A at 230 V: 0.4 seconds for TN systems and 0.2 seconds for TT systems. Advantages of CBs: tripping characteristics are set by the installer, protection is difficult to interfere with, they provide discrimination, and a faulty circuit can be restored easily and quickly by an unskilled operator. Disadvantage: they contain moving parts.
bullets: Thermal: slow, for overload; magnetic: very fast, for fault current
Type B: 3-5 × In (10 A trips at 30-50 A); domestic and light commercial
Type C: 5-10 × In (10 A trips at 50-100 A); commercial and industrial
Type D: 10-20 × In (10 A trips at 100-200 A); industrial high inrush
Table 41.1 (final circuits up to 32 A): 0.4 s TN, 0.2 s TT
CB disadvantage: moving parts

sections.heading: Residual current devices (RCDs)
paragraphs: To detect much smaller leakage currents that could still be lethal, an RCD (BS EN 61008) must be used. It compares the current in the line conductor with the current returning through the neutral. If the difference exceeds a predetermined value, it trips and disconnects the circuit.

The rated value is the IΔn, usually in mA. An RCD does not respond to overload currents. When line and neutral currents are equal, the fields cancel and there is no field in the toroidal core. If some line current flows through earth, there is an imbalance in the core, producing a current in the trip coil.
bullets: Compares line current with neutral return current
Trips if the difference exceeds a predetermined value
Rated value is IΔn, usually in mA
Does not respond to overload currents
Imbalance in the toroidal core gives current in the trip coil

sections.heading: RCBOs
paragraphs: An RCBO (BS EN 61009) is a combination of a thermal-magnetic circuit breaker and an RCD. It gives both overcurrent protection and earth fault protection in a single unit. With most devices two additional wires must be connected for it to function. RCBOs are available in types B and C but not in type D.
bullets: Circuit breaker plus RCD in one unit
Overcurrent and earth fault protection
Most devices need two additional wires
Available in types B and C, not type D

quiz.q: How does BS 7671 Part 2 define overcurrent?
options: A current flowing in the protective conductor
A current exceeding the rated value
A current below the rated value
A current returning through the neutral
quiz.why: Overcurrent is defined as a current exceeding the rated value.

quiz.q: Overload current is an overcurrent occurring in which kind of circuit?
options: One with an insulation failure
One that is short-circuited
One with a broken protective conductor
One which is electrically sound
quiz.why: Overload current occurs in a circuit which is electrically sound.

options: The part including the fuse element(s) that must be replaced after the fuse has operated
The movable part that carries the fuse
The part of the plug that holds the cable
The coloured label showing the rating
quiz.why: The fuse link includes the element(s) and is replaced after the fuse has operated.

quiz.q: Which fusing factor is quoted for BS 88-3:2010 cartridge fuses?
quiz.why: BS 88-3:2010 cartridge fuses have a fusing factor of 1.6-1.9.

quiz.q: Which is a disadvantage of a BS 3036 semi-enclosed fuse?
options: It has moving parts
The element can scatter
It is simple to check if blown
It is costly to replace the element
quiz.why: The element can scatter; the other options are advantages or not stated.

quiz.q: What does the cartridge fuse in a BS 1363 plug protect?
options: The flexible cord
The appliance itself
The socket outlet only
The distributor's cable
quiz.why: The purpose of the plug fuse is to protect the flexible cord, not the appliance.

quiz.q: At what current is a 10 A Type B circuit breaker designed to trip?
quiz.why: Type B trips at 3-5 times In, so a 10 A device trips at 30 A-50 A.

quiz.q: Where are Type C circuit breakers generally used?
options: Domestic installations with low surge currents
Commercial and industrial applications with fluorescent lighting and motors
Only where X-ray machines are used
Only for plug-top protection
quiz.why: Type C (5-10 times In) is generally used in commercial and industrial applications with fluorescent lighting, motors, etc.
